en: I. Introduction.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Now, while a great number of bhikṣus were seated together and assembled in the Karīrikamaṇḍalavāṭa, this kind of conversation arose among them.
It is wonderful, venerable sirs, how far the Blessed One’s perfect individual knowledge and vision extends regarding the past Perfectly Awakened Ones—

those who have passed away, whose course has been cut off, whose veil is torn asunder, who are free from conceptual proliferation, who have transcended proliferation, who have entered final Nirvana, who were compassionate and free from desire.
Such is the way his perfect individual knowledge and vision proceeds.
"Indeed, those Blessed Buddhas were of such a character; they were of such a nature, of such wisdom, of such supernormal powers, of such liberation, and of such a mode of dwelling.
Is it that the Blessed One has thoroughly penetrated the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), or do the deities announce this to him, whereby [he knows] regarding the Tathāgata’s past?

Regarding the Perfectly Awakened Ones who have passed away into the state of non-existence—whose paths are severed, whose coverings are rent asunder, who are free from conceptual proliferation and have transcended proliferation, who have entered final nirvāṇa, who are compassionate and free from desire—in this way, right knowledge and vision arise within oneself:
"Alas, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possessed such ethical discipline; they were of such a nature, such wisdom, and such supernormal powers."

"Ah, how those Blessed Buddhas were thus liberated and thus dwelt!"—this was the conversation that arose among those many monks as they sat together and gathered in the Karīrika Maṇḍalavāṭa. The Blessed One, having retired for his midday rest, heard this with his purified divine ear, which surpasses that of humans; and having heard it, he [approached].
Then, having emerged from that samādhi, he went to where the Karīraka training ground was; having arrived,
he sat down on a seat prepared in front of the community of monks.

Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, what was the conversation that arose among you many monks as you were sitting together and assembled in the Karīrika maṇḍalavāṭa? And with what topic are you now sitting together and assembled?"
"Venerable sir, while we many monks were sitting together and assembled here in the Karīrika maṇḍala enclosure,

this kind of conversation arose among us: 'It is wonderful, venerable friends, how far back the Blessed One's [knowledge extends] regarding the past perfectly awakened ones who have passed away, whose course has been cut off, whose continuity is severed, and who have transcended conceptual proliferation.'"
When those compassionate ones, free from expectations, have passed into final nirvāṇa beyond all conceptual proliferation, there arises within each individual such a right knowledge and vision:

"Indeed, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possessed such virtue; they indeed possessed such Dharma, such wisdom, such supernormal knowledges, such liberation, and indeed dwelt in such a state. Thus they reflect.

Has the Blessed One thoroughly penetrated the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), or do the deities inform him, by which means he [knows] regarding the Tathāgatas of the past— those Perfectly Awakened Ones who have passed away, whose existence has ceased, whose paths are cut off, whose coverings are removed,

who are free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), who have transcended proliferation, who have entered final nirvāṇa, who were compassionate and free from desire, and who thus correctly realized it within themselves?

"Knowledge and vision arise [in them], thinking: 'Ah, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were indeed of such character; they were indeed of such Dharma, such wisdom, such supernormal powers, such liberation, and such a mode of dwelling.
This, venerable sir, was the conversation among us many bhikṣus as we were seated together and assembled at the Karīrikamaṇḍalavāṭa."

“Blessed One, because that intermediate conversation was interrupted, even though the monks are now seated and assembled here, and although the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) has been well-penetrated by me and the deities inform me of this, such is the nature of things (dharmatā) in this matter; therefore, this is said.”
Previously, a righteous discourse connected with the goal was recited by the monks in the circular assembly hall;
indeed, he heard it with his divine faculty of hearing.
Having gone for his midday rest, the Great Sage,
the Teacher, having perceived with his divine ear that the monks had approached the assembly hall, [went there].
For he sat down in the midst of the assembly of monks,
just as Śakra sits among the Tridaśas; the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) was penetrated by the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun.
By which the Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme among bipeds, knows those who have passed away:
their names, their birth, and their clans as they were;
in whatever manner they existed, the Sage has prophesied them all.
Gods of various long lifespans, endowed with beauty and renown, thus proclaim this matter to the illustrious, perfectly awakened ones. 5.
II. How was the Dharmadhātu Realized? How was the dharmadhātu thoroughly penetrated? A. The Characteristics of the Seven Buddhas.
This is the ninety-first eon from now, the eon in which the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin appeared in the world;
this is the thirty-first eon from now, the eon in which the Perfectly Awakened Ones Śikhin and Viśvabhū appeared in the world.

In this very Fortunate Aeon (Bhadrakalpa), four perfectly enlightened Buddhas have appeared in the world: Krakasunda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and we ourselves now as Śākyamuni. This is the natural law (dharmatā) in this matter; therefore, it is said:
And what was that eon, when Vipaśyin appeared,
and [when] Viśvabhū appeared?
The Vināyakas were Krakasunda... [and so forth]. 2. The lifespan of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin was eighty thousand years; the lifespan of the Perfectly Awakened One Śikhin was...

and even now, our lifespan measure is one hundred years, being maintained in perfect happiness—this is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard.

6. Regarding the Assembly of Bhikṣus:
There were three great assemblies of the disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin. One great assembly consisted of six million two hundred thousand bhikṣus.
The second great assembly consisted of one hundred thousand monks; the third great assembly consisted of eighty thousand monks.

For the disciples of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Śikhin, there were three great assemblies: the first great assembly consisted of one hundred thousand monks, the second great assembly consisted of eighty thousand monks, and the third great assembly consisted of seventy thousand monks.

The perfectly enlightened Buddha Viśvabhū had two great assemblies of disciples: one great assembly consisted of seventy thousand monks, and the second great assembly consisted of sixty thousand monks.
The perfectly enlightened Buddha Krakasunda had one great assembly of disciples consisting of forty thousand monks.
There was one great assembly of disciples of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kanakamuni, consisting of thirty thousand bhikṣus.
There was one great assembly of disciples of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kāśyapa, consisting of twenty thousand bhikṣus.
And now, for us as well—(MAV 42)
There was one great assembly of disciples consisting of twelve hundred and fifty monks; this is the natural law (dharmatā) in such cases, and therefore it is said:
There were three [stūpas] for Vipaśyin, three for Śikhin, and three for the Jina Viśvabhū;
for each of these four Buddhas, there was one [stūpa].
The assemblies of seers were revealed by the Sage;
those assemblies of those who perceive the ultimate truth [were held] among the Nāgas... [by the Nāga].
Of all those who belong to the Saṅgha, the Protectors, whose banner is the earth, who are free from passion, and who are upright.
7. The Pair of Disciples of Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One: Khaṇḍa and Tiṣya were his pair of disciples, a foremost pair, an auspicious pair;
one was foremost among those possessing supernormal powers, and the second was foremost among those possessing wisdom. Of Śikhin, the Perfectly Awakened One, [the pair was] Abhibhū...

Under the Perfectly Enlightened One Saṃbhava, there was a pair of disciples, an excellent pair, a blessed pair: one was foremost among those possessing supernatural powers, and the second was foremost among those possessing wisdom. Under the Perfectly Enlightened One Viśvabhū, there was a pair of disciples, Śroṇa and Uttara, an excellent pair, a blessed pair: one was foremost among those possessing supernatural powers, and the second was foremost among those possessing wisdom. [Likewise] under Krakasunda... [there was a pair of disciples...]
The Perfectly Enlightened One Saṃjīva had a pair of disciples, Saṃjīva and Vidura, who were the foremost pair, the auspicious pair;

one was foremost among those with supernormal powers, and the second was foremost among those possessed of wisdom. The Perfectly Enlightened One Kanakamuni had a pair of disciples, the monks Bhujiṣya and Uttara, who were the foremost pair, the auspicious pair; one was foremost among those with supernormal powers.

Of those possessing supreme wisdom, there were two foremost disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa: Tiṣya and Bharadvāja; they were the foremost pair, the auspicious pair. One was foremost among those possessing supernormal powers and the second was foremost among those possessing wisdom. Even now, for us as well, the monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana are the foremost pair, the auspicious pair; one is foremost [among those possessing supernormal powers].
He is the foremost among those possessing supernormal powers and the second foremost among those possessing wisdom; this is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard, and therefore it is said:
Khaṇḍa and Tiṣya were the foremost disciples of Vipaśyin;
Abhibhū and Saṃbhava were those of the Buddha Śikhin; and Śroṇa and Uttara were those of the Jina Viśvabhū.
Having crossed the floods and being unattached to the realms of desire and existence,
these two— the monk Saṃjīva and the wise Vidura— were the foremost disciples of the Teacher Krakasunda.
And here, under the Buddha Kanakamuni, were the two foremost disciples,
the monks Bhujiṣya and Uttara;
and under the Great Seer Tiṣya, the pair Bharadvāja.
These two, the monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, were the foremost disciples of the Blessed One Kāśyapa;
they were the two chief śrāvakas of Aṅgiras.

8. The attendants of the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipaśyin were the monk named Aśoka; the attendant of the Perfectly Enlightened One Śikhin was the monk named Kṣemakāra; [the attendant] of the Perfectly Enlightened One Viśvabhū was Upaśānta.

There was a monk named Nāma who was the attendant of the Perfectly Awakened One Krakasunda; there was a monk named Bhadrika who was the attendant of the Perfectly Awakened One Kanakamuni; there was a monk named Svastika who was the attendant of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa; and there was a monk named Sarvamitra who was our attendant.
Even now, the monk Ānanda is his attendant; this is the natural law (dharmatā) in such cases, and therefore it is said:
Aśoka, Kṣemakāra, Upaśānta, Bhadrika, Svastika, Sarvamitra, and Ānanda is the seventh—
these, O monks, are the great-souled ones who bear their final bodies.
The attendants were skilled in the signs of the mind;
all were proficient in time and penetrating in their discernment of signs.
All their outflows were exhausted, and for them there was no further becoming.

9. The son of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Vipaśyin was named Susaṃvṛttaskandha; the son of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Śikhin was named Atula; the son of the perfectly enlightened Buddha Viśvabhū was named Suprabuddha.
The Perfectly Awakened One Krakasunda had a son named Pratāpana; the Perfectly Awakened One Kanakamuni had a son named Sārthavāha; the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa had a son named Vijitasena;
and for us as well, even now, there is a son named Rāhula. This is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard; therefore, it is said:
Susamvrttaskandha, Atula, Suprabuddha, Pratapana, Sarthavaha, Vijitasena, and Rahula is the seventh—
these are the high-souled sons who bear their final bodies.
The outflows of all have been exhausted; for them, there is no further becoming.
10. Mother, Father, King, and the Capital.
The father of the Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin, was a consecrated Kṣatriya king named Bandhumat.

His mother was named Bandhuvatī, and the capital city was named Bandhumāvatī; it was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and densely populated by many people. The father of the perfectly enlightened Śikhin was a consecrated Kṣatriya king named Aruṇa, and his mother was named Prabhāvatī.

There was a royal capital named Aruṇāvatī; it was prosperous as before. Viśvabhū, the perfectly enlightened one, had a father named King Supradīpa, a Kṣatriya consecrated by coronation, and a mother named Uttarā. There was a royal capital named Anopamā, which was as described before.

The father of the Perfectly Awakened One Krakasunda was a brahmin named Agnidatta, who served as the royal chaplain; his mother was named Dhanavatī. At that time, there was a king named Kṣema, and for King Kṣema, the capital city was named Kṣemāvatī, just as previously described.

The father of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kanakamuni was a brahmin named Yajñadatta, who served as the royal chaplain; his mother was named Yaśovatī. At that time, there was a king named Śobha, and for King Śobha, the capital city was named Śobhavatī, as described previously. The father of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa was Brahmadatta.

The brahmin purohita was named [Viśvāmitra], and his mother was named Viśākhā. At that time, there was indeed a king named Kṛkī; for King Kṛkī, the capital city was named Vārāṇasī, as previously described. Even now, our father is a consecrated kṣatriya king named Śuddhodana, and our mother is named Mahāmāyā; the city is Kapilavastu.

The royal capital named [Kapilavastu] was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants; this is the natural law regarding the tribal republic of the Śākyas, and therefore it is said:
The father of the supreme Buddha Vipaśyin was Bandhumā, and his mother was Bandhuvatī; likewise,
there was the most delightful city of Bandhumatī.
Wherein the Jina taught the auspicious Dharma:
Aruṇa was the father and Prabhāvatī the mother of the Buddha Śikhin, the light-maker.
The city of Aruṇavatī was likewise most delightful,
belonging to King Aruṇa, the crusher of enemies,
from whom the Kṣatriya Supradīpa was born.
The father of the Jina was Viśvabhū;
likewise, his mother was named Uttarasatya, and the capital city was Anopamā. 3.
Agnidatta was born as the brahmin father of the Teacher Krakasunda,
and his mother was also named Dhanavatī, true to her name.
King Kṣema reigned and the royal capital was Kṣemāvatī;
there, the brahmin Yajñadatta was born as the father of the Jina Kanakamuni.
And his mother was Yaśovatī, true to her name;
Śobha was the king, and Śobhāvatī the royal capital,
when the brahmin Brahmadatta was born.
The father of the Blessed One Kāśyapa was [Kṛkī];
his mother was Viśākhā, whose name was true; King Kṛkī was the ruler, and Vārāṇasī was the royal capital. 6.
The father of the Great Seer was named Śuddhodana,
and the mother of Prabhākara was Mahāmāyā; likewise, the city was prosperous, flourishing, and most delightful.
Wherein the Jina named Kapila attained [nirvana].

B. The Legend of Vipaśyin Buddha, Part One: [The Bodhisattva’s Entry into His Mother’s Womb]
1. The Descent from Tuṣita Heaven:

It is the natural law that at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, having passed away from the Tuṣita host of gods, descends into his mother’s womb, at that very moment there was a great earthquake of the earth, and this entire world [was illuminated].
The world was suffused with a sublime radiance; even those intermediate spaces between worlds, which are blind darkness, utter gloom, and impenetrable obscurity—

where even these two, the sun and the moon, despite their such great power and majesty, do not prevail with their light— even those places were at that time suffused with a sublime radiance, and the beings who had been born there...

By means of that light, beings recognize one another: "Other beings, too, have been born here; other beings, too, have been born here. This is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard; therefore, this is said.
Just as a vast, well-filled cloud, laden with much water and stirred by the force of the wind,
so did the Sage enter the womb.
Like the sun approaching a flash of lightning,
he illuminated the people on all sides,
as well as the vast intermediate spaces between worlds shrouded in darkness.
Just as it was unbearable when it ascended into his belly, so too was it here;
this is the natural law (dharmatā) in this matter. 2.
[In His Mother’s Womb] 2. The Four Devaputras.
It is the nature of things (dharmatā) that at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin descended from the Tuṣita heaven-realm into his mother’s womb...

He remained in the womb; then Śakra, the lord of the gods, stationed four sons of the gods as protectors of the mother so that no one—whether human or non-human—might harm her. This is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard; therefore, this is said.
Those sons of the gods, together with the illustrious Śakra, who follow the great-souled deities in the four directions,
were addressed by him as they perceive the ultimate truth.
Provide protection for the mother of the Sugata,
with weapons, missiles, and swords drawn in hand, brandishing spears of extremely sharp form.
May neither humans nor even rākṣasas harm the Mother of the Sugata;
she is protected by the gods and guarded by the most excellent beings.
Glorious and well-guarded by hosts of gods, she sports like an apsaras in the Nandana grove;
such was the natural state of things there. 3.
3. He is as pure as a jewel.

Indeed, at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin descended from the Tuṣita host of gods and took his place in his mother’s womb, he remained there as if enclosed within a sheath, unstained by the impurity of the womb, the impurity of mucus, or the impurity of blood.
Or, for example, if a precious gem were placed near a common, impure object such as a piece of Kāśī cloth,
the precious gem would not be defiled by the Kāśī cloth, nor would the Kāśī cloth be defiled by the precious gem; this is the nature of things (dharmatā) here,
and therefore it is said:
Just as that radiant jewel is not defiled by the finest, most pure Kashi cloth,
so too is the Supreme among Men when he has entered the womb.
The wise one is not defiled by what is made impure.

4. He is like an eight-faceted gem. It is the nature of things (dharmatā) that at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin descended from the Tuṣita host of gods and took his place in his mother’s womb, his mother saw him entirely complete within her womb, just like an eight-faceted beryl gem.
Suppose there were a pearl, pure, translucent, and unclouded, strung upon a five-colored thread—blue, yellow, red, white, and madder-red.
A man with sight, seeing it, would know: "This is the thread; this is the jewel; the jewel is strung upon the thread. This is the natural order of things here; therefore, this is said.
Just as that great Vaiḍūrya jewel is radiant and resembles the rays of the sun,
so too was the Supreme among Men situated within her womb.
The mother of Vipaśyin beholds it in its entirety.
5. He Does Not Fatigue His Mother:

It is the natural law (dharmatā) that at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin descended from the Tuṣita host of gods into his mother’s womb, his mother did not at that time become weary of body or exhausted of body on account of the Bodhisattva.
This is the natural law (dharmatā) maintained here; therefore, this is said.
And he, having descended from [the Tuṣita heaven] by the power of karma, entered her womb;
that she bore him— this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) in this case.
6. His Mother Observes the Five Precepts.

It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, having passed away from the Tuṣita heaven, descended into his mother’s womb, his mother undertook the five precepts (*pañca vratapadāni*) for the rest of her life, [vowing] "for as long as I live, of him..."

The mother abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from unchaste conduct, from false speech, and from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants; this is the natural law in this regard, and therefore this is said.
She did not take what was not given,
she did not speak falsely, she did not drink intoxicants,
and she abstained from unchastity and sexual intercourse.
This is the natural law regarding the mother of Vipaśyin.
7. His Mother Has No Mental Attachment:

It is the nature of things that at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin descended from the Tuṣita host of gods into his mother’s womb, his mother did not thereafter harbor any mental attachment toward men, namely that which is associated with the qualities of sensual pleasure.
This is the natural law in this regard; therefore, this is said:
And when he is not attached even to that,
then his mind is not consumed by the cause of desire,
nor does his mind [long] for a man [in place of] his mother.
It is bound to that which is associated with the qualities of sensual desire.
[The Bodhisattva’s Birth] 8.
Regarding the nature of things (dharmatā) at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin emerged from his mother’s womb, it was exceedingly...
At that time, there was a great earthquake, and this entire world became suffused with a sublime radiance, as previously described, until:
"Other beings as well have been born here. This is the natural law (*dharmatā*) in this regard; therefore, it is said:
As he was being born, the earth trembled and a vast radiance spread forth;
[the world] shone with splendor.
Thus it was; this is the natural law (dharmatā) here.
9. The Newborn Bodhisattva is Born Without Stain.

It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin emerged from his mother’s womb, he emerged like a sword drawn from its scabbard—untainted by the impurity of the womb, the impurity of mucus, the impurity of blood, or any other such impurity.
This is the natural law here regarding that which is impure and elemental; therefore, this is said.
Just as that jewel-gem is luminous and unsullied by the most pure Kashi cloth,
so too is it like gold from the Aṃśuka mine, thoroughly refined.
10. His Mother Gives Birth While Standing.

It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that at the time when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin emerged from his mother’s womb, his mother was neither sitting nor lying down; while standing, that Kṣatriya woman gave birth to the Kṣatriya. This is the natural law in this regard.
Therefore, this is said:
That Kṣatriya woman was neither sitting nor lying down; she remained standing, O you whose valor in truth is supreme. [She] ... [was] ... [like] a lotus. [O you] of excellent truth and prowess!
The god who is the lord of the gods, being eager, seized him.
[After the Bodhisattva’s Birth] 11. He Takes Seven Steps:
It is the natural law that immediately upon his birth, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin took seven steps, supported by no one, and gazed toward the four quarters while uttering these words:
"This shall be my final birth; the gods hold up for me a white parasol with a jeweled handle and a fly-whisk—this is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard; therefore, this is said."
For as soon as he is born, he takes seven steps and utters a word concerning the world; he is the most excellent,
the supreme, the foremost, the highest, the best, and the unsurpassed.
O gods, you who are the protectors of the world!
12. Warm and Cool Streams Fall from Above:

It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that as soon as the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was born, two streams of water fell from the sky—one cool and one warm—which bathed the Bodhisattva. This is the natural law; therefore, this is said.
When the prince was born, endowed with the six great marks,
two streams of water fell from the sky—
one warm and one cool— and pure.
Having bathed, he, the best of bipeds, [is] ... //
13. A Stream Manifests from a Well:

It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that, immediately upon the birth of the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, a great well appeared before his mother, the progenitor, flowing with water from which his mother performed her need for water;
this is the natural law in this regard.
Therefore, this is said:
The Nāgas always perform worship for him in whose mouth a Bodhisattva is born;
they are thrilled, satisfied, joyful, and elated.
In this world, one creates water and then a well.
14. The Deities Scatter Flowers and Play Music.

It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that as soon as the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was born, deities from the sky scattered divine blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), night-blooming water lilies (*kumuda*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), as well as divine powders of *agaru*, *tagara*, and sandalwood (*candana*).
They scattered divine mandārava flowers, played celestial musical instruments, and waved their garments; this is the natural law (dharmatā) in such cases, and therefore it is said:
When the prince was born, endowed with great auspicious marks, having beheld his majesty... [the earth shook].
Until Sujāta, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
shall fulfill the royal succession.
Thus here, the gods dwelling in Akaniṣṭha [utter] the syllables ā _ ^ _ _ ^ ṣv aghoṣa _ ^ X three times.

Part Two [Continuation of the Account Following the Bodhisattva’s Birth] 1. His Wet Nurse
Now, it is the natural law that when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin has been born, his parents entrust him to a nurse, saying:

"O nurse, this prince must be anointed with unguents from time to time, bathed from time to time, fed from time to time, and properly cared for with comfort from time to time. Thus [they charge] the nurse with him.

Having received him with both hands, she anoints him from time to time, bathes him from time to time, feeds him from time to time, and attends to him properly and comfortably from time to time. Furthermore,
having now anointed him with those fragrances in the world that are pleasing to the mind, and having adorned him with all ornaments, she presents him to her father, Bandhumat.
King Bandhumā, having taken him onto his lap and seated him there, gazes at him again and again, giving rise to joy; this is the natural law (dharmatā) in such cases, and therefore it is said:
He gave [the fruit] to his nurse; from her also, [it was given] to the king, and thus it reached the queen herself. 1.103b–c (Yati)

[The Thirty-two Marks of a Great Man] What are those thirty-two marks of a great man possessed by which a great man has two destinies, as previously stated, until: "his fame resounds throughout the world"?
"O King, the prince has well-placed feet; this is a mark of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). 1.
On the soles of his feet, wheels have appeared with a thousand spokes, hubs, and rims, complete in every aspect; this is a mark of a Great Man. 2.
O King, the prince has long fingers; this is a mark of a Great Man. 3. He has broad heels."
"O Prince, this is a mark of a Great Man: (4) his hands and feet are soft and tender;

O Prince, his hands and feet are so soft that they are like a tuft of *tūla* cotton or a tuft of *karpāsa* cotton—this is a mark of a Great Man. (5) His hands and feet are webbed; O Prince, there is a web between his fingers and toes, just like that of a noble king of swans—this is a mark of a Great Man."

"O Lord, the prince has feet with high-arched insteps; this is a mark of a Great Man of a Great Man. (7) O Lord, the prince has calves like those of the eneya antelope; this is a mark of a Great Man of a Great Man. (8) O Lord, the prince has an unbent body;
with his unbent body he can touch and rub both kneecaps; this is a mark of a Great Man of a Great Man. (9)"

O King, the prince has the private organ withdrawn into a sheath; his private organ is enclosed in a sheath, just like that of a noble, well-bred elephant or a noble, well-bred horse—this is a mark of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). O King, the prince is symmetrical like a banyan tree (*nyagrodha*); as far as his body extends, so does his span, and as far as his span extends, so does his body—this is a mark of a Great Man. O King, the prince has body hairs growing upward; this is a mark of a Great Man. O King, the prince has single hairs growing from each pore...
O Prince, each single hair on his body grows individually, blue in color, curled, and turning to the right; this is a mark of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa). 13.
O Lord, the Prince is golden-colored, with skin like refined gold; this is a mark of a Great Man. 14.
The divine prince has delicate skin;

"Come, I shall proclaim the marks of the Great Sage,
who has cultivated his self within this body and now bears his final physical form:
beneath both his feet, two wheels have appeared, perfectly formed."
He has long fingers, and his heels are broad;

His private organ is sheathed within a sheath;

He has a broad and slender tongue, as well as a Brahma-voice;

And these thirty-two marks were developed upon the body of the Great Sage, who had cultivated his self and was bearing his final physical form—
those thirty-two marks which had been fully perfected in him.
In this body there arise two kinds [of rulers]:

Possessing mindfulness, having many sons, with little affliction, and wise, he obtains food, drink, clothing, bedding, and seats;
his retinue is indivisible, and he is pleasing to all embodied beings. (13)
The gods and likewise human beings follow such a person as he is.
Such a mortal would become the foremost among great lords; O Leader, he would be unequaled, peerless, and incomparable. 14–15.
3. His Mother Passes Away.

It is indeed the natural law (*dharmatā*) that seven days after the birth of the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, his mother, the progenitor, passes away; immediately upon passing away, she is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa host of gods. This is the natural law in this regard. Therefore, this is said:
Having indeed carried [the child] in her womb for ten months, the mother of Vipaśyin gave birth to the peerless one;
upon the dissolution of the body, she was reborn among the Thirty-three gods.
The host of gods is the progenitor of the Blessed One.
4. The Physical Beauty of the Bodhisattva:
It is the very nature of things that as soon as he was born, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was handsome, beautiful to behold, and serene;
he surpassed human complexion and had not yet attained divine complexion, such that both men and women gazed upon him.

They do not reach satiety, for his complexion was flawless, just like golden coins made of Jāmbūnada gold, polished by a skilled smith’s son and placed upon a beaten white woolen cloth, which shine, glow, and radiate intensely; even so, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, immediately after birth, was handsome, beautiful to behold, and possessed of such flawless complexion. This is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard; therefore, it is said:
The young boy was as if fashioned by thought alone, like a golden image completed by a skilled craftsman; indeed,
both men and women gazed upon him.
They do not reach satiety with that which is of unimpaired color.
5. The Attractiveness of the Bodhisattva:

Indeed, as soon as he was born, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was dear and pleasing to the great multitude of people; even now, the great multitude of people pass him from shoulder to shoulder, just as they find a autumnal lotus dear and pleasing to the great multitude of people.

And even now, the great multitude of people rubs hand against hand; in the very same way, as soon as he was born, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was dear and pleasing to the great multitude of people, and even now the great multitude of people shifts shoulder against shoulder. This is the natural law (*dharmatā*) in this matter; therefore, this is said.
At that time, while still a youth, Vipaśyin was dear and pleasing to the great multitude;
they walked with one shoulder following the other.
Like a well-grown autumn lotus.
[The Bodhisattva’s Youth] 6. The Bodhisattva’s Eyes Do Not Blink: It is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin beholds forms with unblinking eyes; he does not blink.
Just as it is with the gods reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, this is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard; therefore, this is said.
For this prince does not blink as he gazes upon these delightful forms here, just like the gods who have been reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Moreover, even upon seeing things that are unpleasant.
7. Regarding his maturation:

Indeed, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was endowed with a divine eye born of the ripening of karma, by which he saw equally during both day and night for a distance of one yojana; this is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard. Therefore, this is said:
The Bodhisattva possessed a divine eye, born of karmic maturation, which was purified, stainless, and radiant, by means of which he saw.
And by day and by night, for a full league in every direction.
8. The Beauty of His Voice:
It is the natural law that the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin possessed a beautiful voice and a pleasing voice;
he spoke with the charming speech of a kalaviṅka bird and had the resonance of a drum, just as the Himalayan bird possesses a beautiful voice and a pleasing voice.

And he was one who spoke with the charming voice of a kalaviṅka bird and possessed the resonance of the sound of a drum; in this very same way, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin had a beautiful voice, a charming voice, spoke with the charming voice of a kalaviṅka bird, and possessed the resonance of the sound of a drum—
this is the natural law (dharmatā) in this regard, and therefore it is so stated.
Just as that bird from the Himalayas warbles, intoxicated by the nectar of flowers, even so does he speak with the sweet and melodious voice of a kalaviṅka.
And he too became one who spoke without opposition.

9. Regarding the nature of things (*dharmatā*), the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was indeed wise, discerning, and intelligent; he was endowed with a wisdom that was analytical and investigative like a weaver’s shuttle. Even now, while sitting at his father Bandhumat’s council for the settlement of affairs, he [discerned] profound matters.
This is the nature of things (dharmatā) in this regard; therefore, this is said.
Like an ocean that has drunk the water-bearing clouds, he gave instruction at the residence of Bandhumatī.
He bestowed [his favor] upon many people, the inhabitants of the countryside, and the Kṣatriyas,
out of compassion for their welfare.
Then there arose this proclamation: "Bhadrika!
Furthermore, [he is] Vipaśyin, the one with all-seeing eyes."
10. The Four Excursions [Upon Seeing an Old Man].
It is the nature of things that when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin desired to go out to the pleasure gardens, he addressed his charioteer:
"Charioteer, harness the auspicious vehicle quickly; I shall go out to the pleasure grove.

"So be it, Your Majesty," the charioteer replied to the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin. Having quickly harnessed the auspicious vehicle, he approached the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, and having approached him, he said this to the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin: "It is ready."
"May it be well with the King; let the King depart at whatever time he deems appropriate.

Then the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, having mounted his auspicious vehicle, set out for the pleasure grove. As the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was departing for the pleasure grove, he saw a man who was hunchbacked, with limbs like the rafters of a roof, leaning upon a staff.
Seeing him walking ahead with his body trembling, he addressed the charioteer again:
"Sārathi, why does this man walk ahead with his body trembling, leaning on a staff that is curved like a roof-rafter? His hair is discolored, unlike that of others.
O Deva, this man is called 'old'."
"What is this that is called 'old age,' charioteer?
"Your Majesty, this man must soon die. "What is this that is called 'old age,' Your Majesty? "I too, charioteer, am subject to old age and have not transcended the nature of old age."
"The Prince is also subject to old age and has not transcended the nature of aging.

Therefore, charioteer, turn the chariot back; go toward the inner apartments so that, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, I may contemplate this very matter: that I am indeed not exempt from old age.
The charioteer turned the chariot back and went toward the inner apartments. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin remained within the midst of the inner apartments.
Then, being unacquainted [with this truth], he broods piteously: "I have indeed not transcended old age; this is the nature of things here. Therefore, it is said:
"Having seen here a man whose youth has passed, aged, sickly, gray-haired, and holding a staff..."
Then, being dissatisfied, he meditated on compassion, thinking: "Alas, I have not yet transcended old age."
[The King’s Perturbation 1] Then King Bandhumat addressed his charioteer:
"Charioteer, was the prince pleased when he went to the park? Was he delighted by the park?"
"O King, while the prince was going out to the park grounds, he saw a man who was hunchbacked, bent like a rafter, walking with his body trembling before him while leaning on a staff.

Having seen him, he addressed me: 'Charioteer, why is this man hunchbacked, bent like a rafter, walking with his body trembling before him while leaning on a staff? And his hair is discolored, unlike that of others. To him [I replied]:"

I spoke thus: "Your Majesty, this man is called 'old. He said, 'Charioteer, who is this called "old"? I replied to him, 'Your Majesty, this man will soon have to die; he is what is called "old," Your Majesty.
He said, 'Charioteer, am I also subject to old age, and have I not transcended the nature of old age? I replied to him thus:

"I declare that even a god is subject to old age and has not transcended the nature of aging. He spoke thus: "In that case, charioteer, turn back the chariot; go to the inner apartments. Once I have entered the midst of the inner apartments, I shall contemplate this very matter:
that I, it seems, have not escaped from old age. "O King, that prince, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, was then distressed and uttered piteous cries."
"I am indeed subject to old age and have not transcended it.

Then, this thought occurred to King Bandhumat: "May the words of these Brahmins—those who read omens and are skilled in interpretation—not prove to be true; may it not be that the prince, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes..."

“Having properly clothed himself with robes and having gone forth from home into homelessness out of faith, he will surely renounce the world; what if I were to provide him with an even greater abundance of the five strands of sensual pleasure, so that, being delighted by them, he might not go forth?

Then King Bandhumā provided an even greater abundance of the five strands of sensual pleasure for the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, thinking, “Perhaps he will be delighted and not go forth. This is the natural law (dharmatā) in such a case; therefore—
This is called [the first].
Having heard these words of the attendant,
the father of the beloved Vipaśyin, Bandhuma,
then provided him with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
For he would not renounce those things in which he delights.
[Upon Seeing a Sick Man] It is the natural law that when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin desired to go out to the pleasure gardens, he addressed his charioteer as before, until—
while going out to the pleasure gardens— the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin saw a man who was extremely pale and emaciated.
Seeing one who was rough-skinned, ill-colored, with impaired faculties, and not fit to be looked upon by the eyes of many people, he then addressed his charioteer: "Charioteer,
why is this man so extremely pale, emaciated, rough-skinned, ill-colored, with impaired faculties, and not fit to be looked upon by the eyes of many people?"
"Your Majesty, this man is called 'sick.
What does it mean, charioteer, for him to be called 'sick'?
"Your Majesty, it is possible that this man will die from this very affliction; he, Your Majesty, is what is called 'sick.'"
"Charioteer, I too am subject to disease and have not transcended the nature of disease;
the King as well is subject to disease and has not transcended the nature of disease.

Therefore, Charioteer, turn the chariot back and go toward the inner apartments. Having entered the midst of the inner apartments, I shall contemplate this very matter: that indeed, I have not escaped from disease."

The charioteer turned the chariot back; he went toward the inner apartments. There, now, the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin, having entered the midst of the inner apartments, was dissatisfied and meditated with compassion: "Alas, I have not transcended disease. This is the natural law (dharmatā) in this matter; therefore, it is said:
Having seen here a man afflicted by disease, pale, emaciated, and lacking self-control,
one who is himself undisturbed reflects with compassion.
Indeed, I have not transcended disease.
[The King’s Perturbation 2] Then King Bandhumā addressed his charioteer:

Then eighty thousand monks approached the place where the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin was; having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, they sat down to one side. Those eighty thousand monks, seated to one side, [listened as the Buddha spoke].
The Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin instructed by means of three miracles: the miracle of supernatural power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction.

Being correctly instructed and correctly exhorted by these three miracles, they attained the destruction of the outflows right then and there; this is the natural law in such cases, and therefore it is said:
The ripening of karma,
residing in existence, is experienced in this very life or in future lives.
14. Six More Years of Peregrination.
At that time, a great community of monks—namely, sixty-two hundred thousand monks—resided in the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Then, this thought occurred to the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin: "At present, [this community] is dependent upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī."

A great community of monks dwells here, namely six million two hundred thousand monks. What if I were to exhort my disciples: "Go forth, monks, on your journey for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans; moreover, at the end of six years, you must come to the royal capital of Bandhumatī to hear the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra."
Then the deities dwelling in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, knowing his thought with their own minds, said to the Blessed One:
"At present, a great saṅgha of monks—namely, sixty-two hundred thousand monks—resides depending on the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
May the Blessed One exhort his disciples; I too shall act in such a way that after six years, the monks [will have attained their goal]."
After the passing [of the Buddha], they will come to the capital city of Bandhumatī to hear the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra.
Then the Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin, addressed his disciples:
"Go forth, monks, on your journey for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for its benefit and well-being."

"For the happiness of gods and humans, you should come to the royal capital of Bandhumatī after the lapse of six years to hear the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra. "So be it, Venerable Sir," the monks replied to Vipaśyin, the Perfectly Awakened One, and departed for their travels through the countryside. This is the natural law in such matters; therefore, this is said:
That caravan leader, who was very great,
having been freed from attachment to his disciples by means of [the teaching],
[traveled] from region to region in every direction.

15. When one year had passed, the deities announced: "Venerable sirs, one year of the six years has passed. After the lapse of five years, you must go to the royal capital of Bandhumatī to hear the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra."

When two years had passed, the deities announced: "Venerable ones, when six years have elapsed—after two years have passed and four years have gone by—you must go to the royal capital of Bandhumatī to hear the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra. Then those monks, some by their own power and some by the power of deities, arrived from that very place at the royal capital of Bandhumatī. This is the natural law (dharmatā) in such cases; therefore, this is said.
Desiring to hear the training proclaimed by the Seer, those monks went forth like elephants tormented by thirst.

Patience is the supreme austerity; endurance is what the Buddhas call the highest nirvana;

[Visiting the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven] How do the deities announce [their arrival]?
The thought occurred to me: "I have never before gone there... The thought occurred to me: "I am not [able to go]...

"I shall indeed go to see the Śuddhāvāsa gods; what if I were now to approach the Śuddhāvāsa gods in order to see them?
[Abṛha Heaven]

Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so did I vanish from Jambudvīpa and appear among the Abṛha gods. When the deities of the Abṛha host saw me from afar, they said: "Come, Blessed One!
Welcome, Venerable Sir! From where has the Blessed One come after such a long time? Please be seated."
The Blessed One sat down on the very seat that had been prepared for him, and I likewise sat down on the seat prepared for me.

Then the deities of the Abṛha realm, having bowed their heads at my feet, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, I instructed, inspired, and gladdened the deities of the Abṛha realm with a discourse on the Dharma.
I inspired them and gladdened them.
Then, certain deities from the Abṛha realm rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward me, they said this to me:
"Venerable sir, we are disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin; we were in the presence of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin."

"Having practiced the holy life under Śikhin, we have been reborn here; having practiced the holy life under Viśvabhū, we have been reborn here; having practiced the holy life under Krakasunda, we have been reborn here;

having practiced the holy life under Kanakamuni, we have been reborn here; having practiced the holy life under Kāśyapa, we have been reborn here; and having practiced the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One, we have been reborn here as disciples of the Blessed One.
[From the Ātapa Heaven to the Sudarśana Heaven]

Having thus instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the deities of the Abṛha heaven with a discourse on the Dharma, I entered such a state of meditative concentration that, with my mind thus composed, I vanished from the Abṛha host of gods together with those deities of the Abṛha heaven, and appeared in the Atapa heaven, and so on, up to the Sudarśana heaven.
I established myself as before, up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; "What if I were now to approach even the gods of the Akaniṣṭha realm in order to see them?"
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
even so did I, together with the deities of the Abṛha heaven, together with the deities of the Atapa heaven,
together with the deities of the Sudṛśa heaven, and together with the deities of the Sudarśana heaven, [arrive] in Sudarśana.
Having disappeared from the assembly of gods, I established myself in the Akaniṣṭha realm of the gods.

When the deities belonging to the Akaniṣṭha realm saw me from afar, they spoke thus: "Come, Blessed One! Welcome, Venerable One! From where has the Blessed One come? It has been a very long time since you last made the occasion to visit here; please be seated."
The Blessed One sat down on the very seat that had been prepared for him, and I too sat down on the seat that had been prepared for me;
then the deities belonging to the Akaniṣṭha realm bowed their heads at my feet and sat down to one side.
As I was seated in seclusion, the deities of the Akaniṣṭha realm showed me the Dharma, exhorted me, inspired me, and gladdened me with a discourse on the Dharma.
Then, certain deities of the Akaniṣṭha realm rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward me, they said this to me:
“Venerable sir, we are disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, [having dwelt] in the presence of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin.”

"Having practiced the holy life under Śikhin, we were reborn here; having practiced the holy life under Viśvabhū, we were reborn here; having practiced the holy life under Krakasunda, we were reborn here; having practiced the holy life under Kanakamuni, we were reborn here; having practiced the holy life under Kāśyapa, we were reborn here; and having practiced the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One, we have been reborn here as disciples of the Blessed One. Having thus instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the deities belonging to the Akaniṣṭha realm with a discourse on the Dharma, I entered such a state of meditative concentration that, while my mind was thus composed, I vanished from the Akaniṣṭha host of gods and reappeared in Jambudvīpa.
Thus do the deities announce; this is the natural law (dharmatā) in this matter, and therefore it is said:
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-out arm or draw it back again,
even so did the heroic Sage, the supreme among bipeds.
Then he approached the hosts of gods known as the Abṛhas;
then he approached the hosts of gods known as the Atapas.
Just as water that remains on a lotus leaf rolls off and is not defiled by it,
even so is the heroic Sage, the supreme among bipeds.
Then he approached the hosts of the Sudṛśa gods,
surrounded by those of the Abṛha and Ātapas realms, together with the Sudṛśa deities.
Indeed, Sudarśana, possessing infinite splendor and blazing with glory,
approached the hosts of gods while being followed by those dwelling in the Pure Abodes.
Surrounded by thousands of deities,
the Jina of infinite complexion and endowed with the marks of a hundred merits arrived at the Akaniṣṭha realm. 5.
The disciples of the supreme Buddha Vipaśyin, who perceive the Dharma and are skilled in discerning the nature of phenomena,

With palms joined in reverence, they approached the Tathāgata;
